newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian Christians stage rally for job quotas.
newsitem.headline: Indian Christians stage rally for job quotas.

text.p: Hundreds of Indian Christians whose ancestors converted from low Hindu castes held a rally on Wednesday demanding job and education quotas.
"Dalit", or oppressed, Christian demonstrators carrying placards reading "We Want Justice" marched towards India's parliament clapping, chanting and singing "We Shall Overcome".

The marchers were stopped by a police barricade about one km (half a mile) from parliament, where they squatted briefly before turning back. Organisers said about 500 people participated in the rally but police put the number at 200.

"When there is such overwhelming support for ending the undeclared apartheid against Christian dalits, what prevents the government from taking the next logical step forward?" a spokesman for the All India Christians People's Forum said.
In 1993, India's Supreme Court ruled that nearly half of all federal government jobs should be reserved for lower castes and some tribes, including a few specified Christian communities.
But India did not include Christians who had converted from low castes and who could be leading better lives because Christianity, unlike Hinduism, has no caste system.
The government already sets aside jobs and seats in state-funded universities for low-caste Hindus who became Sikhs or Buddhists to escape from the hidebound caste system.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 15-party coalition government pledged last June to extend the quotas, or reservations, to dalit Christians.
In largely Hindu India, Christians make up 2.4 percent of the 936 million population, Sikhs two percent and Buddhists 0.7 percent.

In 1990, the federal jobs quota proposal triggered independent India's worst student riots, with upper caste students in northern India setting themselves ablaze, fearing they would be increasingly excluded from government jobs.
Christian groups say about 11 million Christians are converts from low Hindu castes and still deprived of education and white-collar job opportunities, traditionally the privilege of higher castes.
